title: What Martha Reveals About Us
paragraphs:
What Martha Reveals About Us
The Scandal of Being Busy for Jesus While Slowly Drifting Away From Him
There is a question hidden beneath the surface of almost every exhausted believer.
A question few Christians dare to say out loud.
"What if I am doing all the right things... but missing Jesus Himself?"
That question is what makes Martha's story so uncomfortable.
Because if we are honest, most of us are far more like Martha than we want to admit.
We carry burdens no one sees.
We solve problems before anyone asks.
We stay busy because busy feels productive.
But sometimes busy becomes a hiding place.
And that is the scandal hidden inside Martha's story.
Not because Martha did not love Jesus.
That is why this story hurts.
Luke records the moment in Luke 10:38-42. Jesus enters Martha's home. Martha immediately begins serving while her sister Mary sits at His feet listening.
The Greek word Luke uses is περισπάω (perispao), meaning "to be pulled away," "dragged in different directions," or "drawn off course."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Martha was distracted by sin.
It says she was distracted by serving.
Because sometimes the greatest threat to intimacy with Christ is not rebellion.
Things that slowly consume our attention until we find ourselves exhausted, frustrated, resentful, and spiritually empty.
Martha eventually reaches a breaking point.
The pressure inside her finally explodes.
"Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me." (Luke 10:40)
This is no longer about dinner preparations.
This is about a wounded heart.
A heart carrying burdens for so long that it finally believes nobody cares.
Many believers know exactly what that feels like.
You carry responsibilities nobody else notices.
And eventually a dangerous thought sneaks into your mind.
Martha's cry is more relatable than most Christians want to admit.
Yet Jesus responds with extraordinary tenderness.
The original Greek preserves the repetition:
In Jewish culture, repeating someone's name was often an expression of deep affection and compassion.
The same pattern appears when God calls "Abraham, Abraham."
The repetition reveals the heart of God.
"Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary." (Luke 10:41-42)
The word translated "anxious" comes from the Greek μεριμνάω (merimnaō), meaning to be divided internally.
How many believers live there right now?
Jesus does not tell Martha that serving is wrong.
He reveals that serving without abiding becomes dangerous.
Because eventually ministry without intimacy creates burnout.
Mary had chosen something Martha had forgotten.
The text says Mary sat at Jesus' feet.
In Jewish culture this was the posture of a disciple.
She understood something Martha had lost sight of.
Jesus did not come merely to receive service.
In Psalm 46:10, the Hebrew text says:
"Be still, and know that I am God."
The phrase "be still" literally carries the idea of letting go.
Many believers spend their entire lives trying to do things for God while resisting the invitation to simply be with Him.
Martha reveals that spiritual exhaustion is often not caused by doing too little.
It comes from carrying what was never ours to carry.
Trying to be savior instead of servant.
Yet Martha's story does not end in shame.
And that is where the Gospel enters.
Because the Bible is not ultimately about Martha.
The One who entered a broken world full of anxious people.
People trying to earn what could only be received.
Jesus did not come to reward the strongest.
He came to save the weary.
He did not come for those who had everything together.
He came for those falling apart.
The cross is the ultimate proof.
There Jesus carried every burden Martha could not carry.
Every exhausting attempt to prove your worth.
"Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows."
At Calvary, Jesus took what belonged to us so we could receive what belongs to Him.
This is why our theme remains true.
And maybe that is why this story still pierces hearts two thousand years later.
Because Martha is not just a woman in Scripture.
And Jesus is still saying the same words.
But His invitation remains the same.
Before you do something for Jesus, remember that He first wants you with Him.
If this article exposed something hidden inside your heart, be honest.
Your testimony may be exactly what another weary soul needs to read today.
They may see themselves in Martha's story more than they realize.

One day you will discover that the most important moments of your life were not the moments when you were doing the most for Jesus—but the moments when you finally stopped long enough to hear Him call your name.
